en: Preface to the Precepts on Returning [to the Source]: As for the Three Jewels, their nature and characteristics are eternally abiding; their substance pervades the Dharma-realm. They respond to things and adapt to capacities like the sun shining upon a thousand rivers.
Serving as the vessel and rudder for the world, they cannot be compared to the three fears. Therefore, when first setting the mind to enter the Way, one must first...

Take refuge in the Triple Gem and receive the precepts against killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxicants. These resemble the Five Constant Virtues of Confucianism—benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness.
However, while the merit of the Five Constant Virtues is realized within a single lifetime, the efficacy of the Five Precepts extends across many kalpas.

Thus it is said: "If one does not uphold the Five Precepts, the path to the realms of humans and devas is severed. Even the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks of physical perfection were all attained through the observance of the precepts; if one were not...
By upholding the precepts, one will not even obtain the body of a mange-scarred jackal, let alone a body endowed with merit.

If one can uphold the precepts, one will gain renown in the present life and ultimately transcend the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Therefore, we see that by revering the precepts and abstaining from killing, benevolence manifests of its own accord without being pursued;
by upholding the precepts and refraining from theft, righteousness spreads of its own accord without being exalted; and by guarding the precepts and eliminating sexual misconduct...
By practicing ritual, ritual becomes self-established; by following the precepts, delusion ceases. Without seeking faith, faith is spontaneously achieved;

by receiving the precepts and abstaining from alcohol, one does not cultivate wisdom, yet wisdom becomes naturally clear. This reality may be called shaking the net and holding the main cord, whereby the myriad meshes are opened wide.
It shatters the shell of ignorance and brings one out from the dream of the long night. What further merit could possibly be added? What virtue could be greater?
To apply this accordingly: if one does not cultivate [the Way], one remains ignorant of what is truly desired;

in vain one exerts one's thoughts over names and forms, toils the mind with the works of a hundred schools, and exhausts body and spirit through nights and days, leaving the ears and eyes empty during fair mornings. How far removed is this from the Way! How distant it has fled!
How could one fail to reach it? If one attains its root, there is nothing that desire cannot accomplish; if one discards its substance, from where could one apply the mind?
For this reason, the Brahmacārin abandons heterodox teachings and takes refuge in the Triple Gem, while the Bodhisattva upholds the prohibitive precepts.
Yet their rank is equal to that of Great Enlightenment. Regarding such a teaching as this, who could possibly conceive of it?

concerning the Method for Receiving the Three Refuges: After the Tathāgata had attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, he sat in the full lotus posture.
For seven days he remained unmoving, experiencing the bliss of liberation. After the seven days had passed, he arose from his meditative concentration.

Before he had yet eaten, there were two merchant brothers—one named Trapusa and the other Upāli (in other sūtras, one is called Trapuṣa and the other Bhallika)—who were passing by not far from the tree with five hundred wagons laden with wealth and treasures. The tree deity exhorted them [to offer food].
They offered honey-gruel to the Tathāgata. Having heard this, the two men were filled with joy; they immediately took the honey-gruel and offered it to the Tathāgata.
Out of compassion, the Buddha accepted it and then exhorted and transformed them, saying: "O merchants!"
"Now you may take refuge in the Buddha; take refuge in the Dharma. He then received these words of instruction: "Venerable One, I now take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma.
This was the first instance of two people receiving the two refuges among the *upāsakas*. At that time, the two men said to the Buddha:

"I am now returning to my native land. How shall I cultivate merit, pay homage, and make offerings? The World-Honored One immediately gave him his hair and nails, instructing him to take them back and cultivate merit through worship and offerings.

(At that time, as the Sangha did not yet exist, he received the two refuges. Other sutras state: "The Buddha taught, 'You should take refuge in the Sangha,' because the Sangha would exist in the future.

These two men were citizens of the city of Bāhīka, west of the Snowy Mountains. Receiving the Tathāgata’s command, they requested the hair and returned to their respective countries. Each built a stūpa in their own city to make offerings. This was the very first [stūpa] of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.

This is a stūpa. The *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Universal Radiance) states: "The Buddha bestowed predictions upon two individuals that they would become Buddhas in the future, named Mṛgadhvaja Tathāgata.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had consumed the parched grain and honey, he sat cross-legged and remained unmoving for seven days, delighting himself by dwelling in the samādhi of liberation. After seven days had passed, he arose from samādhi.
A tree deity of the harītakī tree, who possessed profound faith in the Buddha, took a harītakī fruit and came to offer it to the World-Honored One.
Out of compassion for him, the Buddha accepted it and said, "Now you take refuge in the Buddha; take refuge in the Dharma.
He replied, "So be it," and thus took refuge in the Buddha and the Dharma. Among all the deities who received the refuges, the deity of the harītakī tree was the first.
When the Buddha had finished eating the fruit, he again entered into *samādhi* for seven days. Rising from *samādhi*, he held his alms bowl.
He entered the village of Uruvilvā to beg for alms. At that time, the daughter of the general Sujātā conceived a heart of joy and came out to offer him food.
Out of compassion for her, the Buddha accepted it and said to her, "Now you take refuge in the Buddha; take refuge in the Dharma. She replied:
"So it is. I now take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma. Among the female lay disciples (*upāsikā*) who received the two refuges, the daughter of the General was the first.
At that time, the Buddha went to the banks of the river where the dragon *Maṇiviṣa* dwelt.

The Dragon King transformed himself into a youth, joined his palms, knelt with one knee on the ground, prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata, and praised the Buddha with a verse. The Buddha said to the Dragon King: "You now take refuge in the Buddha."
“Dharma,” he replied, “it is so. I now take refuge in the Buddha and the Dharma. As for those among the animals who receive the two refuges, the Nāga King Manasvin is their leader.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had accepted the invitation of Brahmā Devarāja to turn the Wheel of the Dharma, he proceeded to the Deer Park in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī and, for the sake of the five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, three times turned the Wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. His mind...
They attained liberation and became arhats; these constitute the Jewel of the Saṃgha, the unsurpassed field of merit for gods and humans.

(Subsequently, he converted Yaśas, the son of Kātyāyana; Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; and the followers of the three Kāśyapas, totaling one thousand two hundred and fifty people. [In the Song edition, "木" is replaced by "取. Later, he entered parinirvāṇa after converting Subhadra. The number of those he converted in the interim is beyond counting. Thus the Sūtra says:

The Buddha told Ānanda, "The Tathāgata’s disciples in the eastern direction are countless billions; the disciples in the southern, western, and northern directions are likewise countless billions. At that time, Yaśas’s father went to see the World-Honored One.
"Venerable One, the Buddha taught me the Dharma, and I immediately attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. I said to the Buddha:
'I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha. I pray only that the World-Honored One will grant me the status of an upāsaka.

From this day forth, for as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from killing, and so on, up to refraining from drinking intoxicants. This was the first instance of the three refuges, [given by] Yaśodharā’s father."
At that time, Yaśodharā’s mother and her wife prepared various kinds of food and drink and offered them to the World-Honored One.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. They addressed the Buddha, saying: "From this day forward, we take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
please accept us as laywomen (*upāsikā*). From this day forward, for as long as life lasts, we shall refrain from taking life, and so on, up to refraining from drinking alcohol. This was [the case].
This refers to the laywomen (*upāsikā*) who first received the three refuges, headed by Yaśodharā and her wife. The *Mahābhiṣeka Sūtra* states:
When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, preaching the Dharma to bhikṣus, bodhisattvas, and the eight classes of beings including devas and nāgas, a deer-headed brahmin arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling.
He prostrated himself in salutation and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I have long heard of the Tathāgata..."
His fame resounded far and wide. Now, wishing to renounce other teachings, he sought to receive the three refuges along with the dharma of the five precepts.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, brahmin! Since you are able to renounce other paths and take refuge in me, you should repent of the sins of birth and death;
its merit shall be immeasurable and beyond calculation. The brahmin replied, "Yes, I accept your instruction," and immediately purified his body and speech.

The Bodhisattva further thought: "I only pray that the World-Honored One will bestow upon me the precepts of the Dharma, which I shall practice and uphold for the rest of my life, never daring to violate or neglect them.

The Buddha said: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time have all spoken these precepts of the Dharma. You should listen attentively and receive them with care; hold them in your mind and keep them in constant recollection."
The Buddha said: "For as long as life lasts, take refuge in the Buddhas, the Unsurpassed Honored Ones; for as long as life lasts, take refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One Free from Desire;
for as long as life lasts, take refuge in the Saṃgha, the Honored One Among the Multitudes. The Buddha said:
"Brahmin, having completed these three refuges, one is a true disciple and shall not be disturbed by evil or wickedness. Thus, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* says: "By..."
The Three Jewels are the refuge; they are intended to provide protection so that one may not be oppressed or harmed. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-śāstra* states:

"The Three Jewels are auspicious and the most excellent, wholesome conditions. Those who take refuge in them can accomplish the great task: they give rise to all roots of goodness, leave behind the suffering of birth and death, and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Now, those who wish to receive [the precepts] must first be taught to pay homage to the Three Jewels and their own Teacher.

To the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, and next to the preceptor, one pays homage and then receives [the precepts]. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, when one is about to receive them, one should fully cultivate dignified deportment.

Upon approaching the ordained person who serves as the preceptor, the preceptor explains the two dharmas of good and evil, causing [the candidate] to discern the heterodox from the orthodox, to give rise to joy for the former and aversion for the latter, and to expand the mind and spirit. Thereafter, he bestows [the precepts], saying:

I, [Name], for as long as life lasts, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha. (Instruct them to recite this three times. Once they have become members of the Dharma, next bestow the Three Bonds.)
I, [Name], for as long as life lasts, have completed my refuge in the Buddha; I have completed my refuge in the Dharma; I have completed my refuge in the Saṃgha (recited three times).
One should know that with the completion of the first three refuges, wholesome dharmas are immediately generated. Once the subsequent three [vows] are concluded, there remains only body and speech;
the self and its attachments no longer exist. Thus, the *Mahā-upāya-sūtra* asks: "What is the nature of the Three Refuges? A treatise states: "It is instruction."

Regarding the nature of non-informative action (*avijñapti*): when one receives the three refuges, kneeling on the right knee with palms joined and verbally reciting the three refuges is called bodily and vocal [informative action].

If there is a mind of pure devotion, there exists bodily and vocal non-informative action; this is what is meant by informative and non-informative action. Therefore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* says:

If one receives [the precepts] with a sincere and earnest mind, both the informative (vijñapti) and non-informative (avijñapti) aspects are present. If one receives them with a disrespectful or casual mind, there is only the informative aspect; the non-informative aspect is absent.

(The "informative and non-informative" refers to the essence of the *karmasamvara*—the precepts of action and non-action. Although these informative and non-informative aspects are called the "Three Refuges," they collectively encompass the essence of all the precepts.

If one receives the Three Refuges alone, it is merely termed "taking refuge in the Dharma" and does not constitute the formal dharmas of the precepts. Therefore, the treatise states: "There is that which..."

Furthermore, one obtains both the Refuges and the Precepts; if there is no conferral, one has the Refuges but not the Precepts. Therefore, the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* clarifies that there are five kinds of the Three Refuges:

first, the Three Refuges for turning away from heterodoxy; second, the Three Refuges for the Five Precepts; third, the Three Refuges for the Eight Precepts; fourth, the Three Refuges for the Ten Precepts;
and fifth, the Three Refuges for the Great Precepts (*mahāśīla*). Regarding what is called the "Three Refuges for the Great Precepts," it refers to when the Buddha first ordained people.

Before the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) was established, there were those who received the Great Precepts (*mahāśīla*) by taking the Three Refuges, and those who became *bhikṣus* through the call "Come, O Well-Come One" (*ehi bhikṣu*).

After the establishment [of the rules], this was no longer permitted. Regarding what is called the "Three Refuges for Turning Away from Evil," it refers to sentient beings who, since beginningless kalpas, have been obstructed by delusion and karma;
they do not recognize the Triple Gem and do not know the way of transcendence. They may rely instead upon celestial deities or non-Buddhist paths, or...
Having relied upon worldly teachings as their refuge, they now first change their minds to take refuge in the True Teaching.

They overturn their former adherence to heterodoxy to establish it as the foundation for cultivating the causes and realizing the fruits of entering the Path. Therefore, the Buddha first had them receive the Three Refuges and only thereafter perform repentance;
this is called the "Three Refuges for Overturning Heterodoxy. Now that they have taken refuge in the Triple Gem, they must necessarily sever evil and cultivate goodness.

Only then may one be rightly called a child of the Buddha. How could it be permissible to continue as before, committing killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, while still claiming the title of *upāsaka*?

Regarding the Buddha: if one recites "Buddha" or "Buddha-Saṅgha," but does not recite "Dharma," does this constitute the Three Refuges? The answer is: in neither case is the Three Refuges accomplished. The Buddha takes the Dharma as his teacher;
the Buddha is born from the Dharma; the Dharma is the mother of the Buddha; and the Buddha abides in reliance upon the Dharma. Question:
If the Buddha takes the Dharma as his teacher, why is the Dharma not placed first among the Three Jewels? The answer is:
although the Dharma is indeed the teacher of the Buddha, the Dharma is not propagated without the Buddha. As it is said, "The Way is propagated by persons.
For this reason, the Buddha is placed first. The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: The elder Sujāta addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, what is meant by..."

Regarding the three refuges, the Buddha said: "Good son, in order to destroy all suffering, sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), and attain the unsurpassed bliss of nirvāṇa, one takes the three refuges for these reasons.
As to what you asked concerning what the three refuges are: they are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
The Buddha is the one who can teach the cause for severing the afflictions and attaining right liberation. The Dharma is..."
This is the cause of affliction. True liberation consists in the Sangha receiving and internalizing that which destroys the causes of affliction, thereby attaining right liberation.
Some may say: "If this is so, then there is only one refuge. This interpretation is not correct. Why?
Because whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the True Dharma always exists. For those who are free from discrimination, when a Tathāgata appears in the world...
There is a distinction. Therefore, one should take refuge separately in the Buddha. Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the True Dharma (saddharma) is ever-present;
yet there is no one to uphold it. Once a Tathāgata has appeared, there is someone to uphold it. Therefore, one should take refuge separately in the Dharma.
Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the True Dharma is ever-present; yet there is no one to receive it. As for...

Once [the Dharma] has been brought forth, there are those who receive it; because the community of the Buddha’s disciples is able to receive and uphold it, one should therefore take refuge separately in the Saṃgha.
Right Path and liberation—this is called the Dharma. One who is self-awakened without a teacher—this is called the Buddha.

One who is able to receive [the teachings] in accordance with the Dharma—this is called the Saṃgha. If these three refuges did not exist, how could one speak of the four kinds of indestructible faith? This is well said.
"O son of noble family, just as the Buddha, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Śrāvaka are each distinct, for this reason the Three Jewels cannot but be distinct.

For what reason is it said that the Buddha is the Dharma? Because one is able to understand this Dharma, one is called a Buddha. Because one receives and explains the analytical teachings, one is called the Saṃgha.

By contemplating conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and seeing their many faults and transgressions, one practices alone and attains the taste of the Deathless (*amṛta*); therefore, [the Buddha is so named]."
Because it is the Buddha, the entirely untainted and unconditioned realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), it is called the Dharma.
Because one upholds the prohibitive precepts and reads, recites, and explains the twelve divisions of the scriptures, it is called the Sangha.

If someone were to say, "After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, what is it that one takes refuge in when taking refuge in the Buddha?"—O son of good family, such a taking of refuge is called taking refuge in the Buddhas of the past.
The Buddha. Regarding the dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is just as I previously instructed the householder Trapusa:

"You should take refuge in the Sangha of future ages; taking refuge in the Buddhas of the past is likewise. Because there are differences in the field of merit and its karmic fruit, they are distinguished into three.
However, whether the Buddha is in the world or has entered *parinirvāṇa*, there is no difference in the fruit and retribution of making offerings. Thus one receives the refuges.
The same applies to those who rely [on the Triple Gem]. Whether male or female, one who can recite the Three Refuges three times is called an upāsaka or upāsikā.
The wise observe deeply that the Tathāgata’s wisdom and liberation are supreme, and he is able to teach liberation.
Furthermore, he can explain the cause of liberation and the state of unsurpassed tranquility; he can exhaust the great ocean of the suffering and affliction of birth and death.
His deportment is dignified and orderly, and his three karmas are serene. Therefore, one should first take refuge in the Buddha. The wise contemplate this deeply.
The phenomena of birth and death are a great mass of suffering; the unsurpassed right path can forever sever them. The phenomena of birth and death are the famine of craving and thirst;
the flavor of the unsurpassed nectar can fully satisfy them. The phenomena of birth and death are fearsome perils and difficulties.

The unsurpassed True Dharma can sever and eliminate these: the errors of birth and death, deviance and incorrectness, seeing permanence in the impermanent, seeing a self in what is not-self, seeing pleasure in what is not-pleasurable, and seeing purity in the impure. The unsurpassed True Dharma is fully capable of severing all such things.
For these reasons, one should take refuge in the Dharma. The wise should observe that the followers of external paths lack shame and remorse, and do not abide according to the Dharma.
Although they practice the way, they do not know the correct path; although they seek liberation, they do not attain the essential method.
Even when they acquire slight worldly virtues, they are stingy and protective of them, unable to explain them to others; thus, their conduct is not virtuous.

Their nature is to conceive thoughts of performing wholesome deeds; they perceive the Buddha and the Saṅgha as tranquil; their minds are filled with great compassion; they have few desires and are content;
they abide in accordance with the Dharma, cultivate the right path, and attain right liberation. Having attained it, they are further able to turn back and explain it to others.
For this reason, one should next take refuge in the Saṅgha. If one can pay homage to these Three Jewels, welcoming them when they come and seeing them off when they depart, and honor and praise them—
Sighing, he dwells in accordance with the Dharma as it truly is, believing it without doubt; this is what is called making offerings to the Triple Gem.

Having received the Three Refuges, if one then performs deluded deeds, accepts the teachings of non-Buddhists, or follows the words of Maheśvara, by these causes and conditions, one loses the Three Refuges.
If a person is upright, their mind free from stinginess and greed, constantly practicing shame and remorse, having few desires and being content—such a person...

Having long attained the body of tranquility (the Dharma-body), if one performs various mixed karmas for the sake of experiencing pleasure and cultivates virtuous deeds according to the principle of market trade, such that the mind cannot have compassion for sentient beings, then such a person does not obtain the Three Refuges.
The Elder Sudatta instructed his household that even those in the womb were all to receive the Refuges. This is...
"A child in the womb does not truly accomplish the taking of refuge. Why is this? Because these teachings must be personally proclaimed by one's own mouth.
Although the refuge is not accomplished [by the unborn], it can nonetheless protect them. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what kind of person obtains the three refuges?"

"Who are those persons who do not obtain the Three Refuges? The Buddha said, "Good son, if a person believes in causes, believes in effects, believes in the Truths, and believes that there is the attainment of the Path—such a person obtains the Three Refuges.

If a person with a sincere heart believes that which cannot be defeated, draws near to the Triple Gem, and receives the instructions of virtuous friends—such a person obtains the Three Refuges, O Upāsaka."
The precepts are likewise thus. If one can contemplate these Upāsaka precepts, they possess immeasurable fruits of merit and reward;
they are able to destroy immeasurable base and evil dharmas. Sentient beings are infinite, and their suffering is likewise so. It is difficult to obtain a human body;
though one obtains a human body, it is difficult to have all faculties complete; though one has all faculties complete, it is difficult to attain faith; and though one attains faith—

The mind [is fickle]. It is difficult to encounter virtuous friends; though one encounters virtuous friends, it is difficult to attain mastery. Though one attains mastery, all phenomena are impermanent.
If I now create evil karma, because of this evil karma, I shall obtain the retribution of evil for both body and mind in two lifetimes.
For these reasons, my own body, speech, and mind are my enemies. Even if the three types of evil karma did not result in evil retribution in the present...
These evils should not be committed. These three evil karmas can produce ugly physical forms and other such misfortunes in the present life, and cause regret at the time of death.
For these reasons, I take refuge in the Triple Gem and observe the eight precepts of the fast, distancing myself from all evil and unwholesome karma.
The wise should contemplate that there are two kinds of precepts: first, worldly precepts; second, ultimate precepts (paramārtha-śīla).
If one receives the precepts without relying upon the Triple Gem, this is called worldly precept; such a precept is not firm, like colored paint without glue.

Therefore, I first take refuge in the Triple Gem and only then receive the precepts—whether for as long as life lasts, or for one day and one night, namely the Upāsaka precepts and the Eightfold Fasting Rite. Indeed, worldly precepts cannot be broken [by external forces].
One can destroy previous evil karmas by receiving the precepts of the Three Refuges. Why is this? It is because of the power and momentum of the precepts. The *Mahā-upāya-sūtra* asks:
"Does one take refuge in Śākyamuni Buddha, or does one take refuge in the Buddhas of the three periods of time? The answer is:

"One takes refuge in the Buddhas of the three periods of time, because the Dharma-body of the Buddhas is identical. To take refuge in one Buddha is itself to take refuge in the Buddhas of the three periods."
Because all Buddhas are non-different from one another. Question: Does one take refuge in the form-body (*rūpakāya*), or does one take refuge in the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)?
Answer: One takes refuge in the dharma-body; one does not take refuge in the form-body, for the form-body is not the Buddha. Question:
If the form-body is not the Buddha, why does shedding the blood of the Buddha’s body constitute a heinous offense (*ānantarya-karma*)? Answer: The form-body is the dharma-body.
Because it is the vessel; because it is the basis of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). If one harms the physical body (*rūpakāya*), one incurs the crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*);
it is not because the physical body is the Buddha that one incurs the crime of immediate retribution. Therefore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śīla-saṃgraha-śāstra* states:

"One who takes refuge in the Buddha takes refuge in the Dharma-body, which is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) consisting of the unlearned virtues (*aśaikṣa-guṇa*) formed by the five factors. One who takes refuge in the Dharma takes refuge in that which exhausts both self and others."

"Place" refers to the cessation of desire and the absence of desire; it is the *nirvāṇa* of the Truth of Cessation (meaning the place where the delusions of oneself and others have been extinguished and are no longer present, hence it is called the "place of exhaustion"). Regarding taking refuge in the Saṃgha:

one takes refuge in the Saṃgha of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which refers to the field of merit that brings forth blessings—namely, the virtues of the Śrāvakas who are in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The *Bao'en jing* asks: "If one takes refuge in the Saṃgha of the Ultimate Truth, then as for the Buddha and Trapusa and Bhallika..."

Regarding the taking of the three refuges for the sake of benefit, one should not say that there will be a Saṃgha in the future. You should take refuge in the Saṃgha of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), which is eternally present in the world.

The answer is: Because the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) Saṃgha is the basis upon which the Saṃgha of the ultimate truth relies, it is said that there will be a Saṃgha in the future, and you should take refuge in it.
Furthermore, such a statement is made out of a desire to show respect for the conventional truth. Thus spoke the Buddha.

He himself declared: "Among all assemblies, the assembly of the Buddha is foremost. If there is an assembly of monks gathered together, within it are those of the four stages of approach and the four fruits of attainment, who constitute the unsurpassed field of merit. Among all ninety-six kinds of assemblies, they are the most honored and supreme."

There is none who can equal him; therefore, it is said that there will be a Sangha in the future, and you should take refuge in them. This does not contradict the correct principle. The Tiantai teachings clarify two kinds of Triple Gem:
first, the Institutional (or Sustaining) Triple Gem; second, the Essential (or Unity) Triple Gem. Regarding the Institutional Triple Gem:

when the Buddha was in the world, his attainment of enlightenment beneath the tree constituted the Buddha-Gem; his preaching of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths constituted the Dharma-Gem; and his ordination of the five bhikṣus constituted the [Sangha-Gem].
The Jewel of the Sangha. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, casting metal or molding clay, and painting with cinnabar and green pigments, constitute the Buddha-Jewel.

Writing upon paper or palm leaves the holy teachings of the Tripiṭaka constitutes the Dharma-Jewel. Shaving the head, donning dyed robes, and continuing to flourish the Buddha’s transformation constitute the Sangha-Jewel.
Because these three sustain [the teaching] without interruption, they are called the "Sustaining Three Jewels. Yet all such images are the true body; this is the Sūtra.
This is where the sacred texts are kept; these are the relics of the Buddha. Even ordinary monks of the present day are able to shoulder the True Dharma and serve as fields of merit for the world;

all should pay them reverence. As for what is called the "Three Jewels in One Substance," this is precisely the single mind. Its self-nature does not return [to a source], nor is there any place to which it returns.
If one uses the wisdom of the true mark to awaken to all phenomena, they are neither empty nor existent, yet both empty and existent.
The simultaneous forgetting and simultaneous illumination of the three wisdoms in perfect enlightenment is called the Buddha Jewel.

The principle of the dharma-nature that is thus realized, complete with the three truths, is called the Dharma Jewel. This enlightened wisdom, in harmony with both principle and phenomena, is called the Sangha Jewel.
For those who wish to practice worship, there is no presiding entity apart from this single essence, nor is there anything apart from the presiding entity itself.

To speak of them as a single essence while remaining attached to their distinct characteristics—if one is ignorant of the principle of the single essence yet performs acts of reverence, one merely attains mundane goodness but cannot be said to perform true worship.

Conversely, if one discards the characteristics of manifestation and maintenance while discussing the single essence, one falls into the emptiness of nihilism and cannot be said to have realized the principle.

This is because by placing the principle outside of phenomena, one fails to understand that the entirety of phenomena is itself the principle; how then could one awaken to the fact that both subject and object are empty of intrinsic nature? Thus, [true resonance] arises...
Should one not consider these as those with whom the Way intersects? Because these Three Jewels abide eternally in the world, they cannot be disparaged or treated with contempt by worldly dharmas;

thus they are called "Jewels" (*ratna*). Just as worldly precious gems are held in high esteem by sentient beings, so too these Three Jewels are that toward which all living beings, the three vehicles, and the seven assemblies look for refuge and veneration;
hence they are named the "Three Refuges" (*triśaraṇa*). The *Ratnagotravibhāga* states: "The three..."
The Jewel has six meanings; therefore, it must be revered. First is the meaning of rarity:

just as worldly treasures cannot be obtained by those who are impoverished, so too the Triple Gem cannot be encountered by beings of meager merit throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes;
this is why it is called a "Jewel. Second is the meaning of being free from defilement: just as genuine worldly treasures have no flaws or impurities in their substance, so it is with the Triple Gem.
Thus it is. Because they are utterly free from all outflows (*āsrava*), they are called "jewels" (*ratna*). Third is the sense of "power":
just as worldly precious jewels have great power to eliminate poverty and neutralize poison, so too the Three Jewels possess the inconceivable power of the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*);
therefore, they are said to be jewels. Fourth is the sense of "adornment": just as worldly precious jewels can adorn the body and head, making the person beautiful, [so too do the Three Jewels].
The Three Jewels are likewise. Because they can adorn the practitioner by purifying their body, they are called "Jewels. Fifth is the sense of being supreme:
just as worldly precious gems are superior among all things, so too are the Three Jewels the most excellent within all worlds;
therefore, they are named "Jewels. Sixth is the sense of being unchanging: just as worldly pure gold cannot be altered by burning, grinding, or smelting...
They undergo transformation; yet the Three Jewels are like this, not altered by the eight worldly dharmas, and for this reason they are called "Jewels.
Thus a sutra says: "The power of the three refuges is greatest; one must receive them. Long ago, the Five Virtues departed from the body of Śakra, Lord of Devas.
Knowing that his life was ending and that he was about to be reborn in the world as a donkey in a potter’s household, he was filled with great sorrow and anxiety.
He thought to himself, "Within the three realms, only the Buddha can deliver beings from their suffering and distress. Thereupon, he hurried to the place where the Buddha was.
He prostrated himself in worship and, lying flat on the ground with a sincere heart, took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha three times.
Before he had even risen, his life suddenly departed, and he was reborn as a child within the womb of a mother donkey at a potter’s workshop.
At that time, the donkey broke loose and ran among the unbaked clay vessels, smashing the pottery. Her master beat her, and she immediately miscarried; the spirit then returned to its former body.

From the midst [of his existence], the merit of his five virtues returned, and he was once again made a Heavenly Lord (Śakra). When the Buddha arose from his meditative concentration, he praised him, saying, "Excellent!

Heavenly Lord, that you were able to take refuge in the Triple Gem at the moment of your death—your karmic retribution is now exhausted, and you shall no longer undergo further toil and suffering. The Buddha then preached the Dharma for him;
the Heavenly Lord received it with joy and attained the stage of Srotāpanna. The *Zhé fú luóhàn jīng* (Sūtra on the Subjugation of Arhats) says: "Long ago, in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven..."
"O Devaputra, your lifespan is nearly exhausted and the five signs of decay have appeared.

Observing what will happen after your death, you see that you will descend to be born in the kingdom of Vaiśālī as the offspring within the womb of a mangy sow. Distressed and unhappy, a deity said to you:

'Only the Buddha can deliver you from this transgression. You immediately went to the Buddha's dwelling and paid homage; before you had even asked a question, the Buddha told the Devaputra: 'All things in the universe..."
"Return to impermanence; this is what you have long known. Why do you grieve? The deva addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Although I know that celestial blessings cannot last long, I regret leaving this seat, for I shall constantly be reborn in a pig's womb. This is what I dread as a poison; I am not afraid of receiving a body in the human realm. The Buddha said:
"If you wish to escape the pig's body, you should recite the Three Refuges. The deva immediately followed the Buddha’s instruction and, from morning until night, practiced it himself.

He returned. When his life span was exhausted after seven days, he descended to be born in the kingdom of Vaiśālī as the son of an elder. While still in his mother’s womb, he took refuge three times a day;
upon being born and falling to the ground, he likewise knelt and took refuge. The entire family was deeply perplexed and called him a malevolent omen (graha), intending to kill him.
Only his father recognized him and said, "This child is no ordinary person. Even those who live a hundred years do not yet understand taking refuge."
The Three Jewels! How much more so when, upon first falling to the ground, he was able to call himself a Buddha; they cared for him with great affection.

When the boy was seven years old, he encountered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana on the road and paid them homage. The assembly was all struck with wonder and astonishment. The boy said, "Do you holy men not recognize me?
While I was in the heavens, I should have been reborn in the evil realms, but because the Buddha granted me refuge, I have obtained birth as a human being. I pray that you..."
I said, "I invite the Buddha and the Sangha. The son returned and informed his parents, saying, "I wish for you to prepare an offering.

His parents were amazed that he, being so young, could give rise to such a great resolve; they rejoiced and prepared it. The Buddha and the assembly of monks arrived by means of their supernatural powers.

He then preached the Dharma for them, and the son, his parents, and all their internal and external relatives all attained the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) and took the threefold refuge.
This is his merit. The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, I do not understand:

what practices did this Bhikṣu of the heavy clan perform in the past, and what roots of goodness did he plant, that he has now appeared in the world and, though falling into water and being swallowed by a fish, does not die?
The Buddha told Ānanda, “In the distant past, a Buddha appeared in the world named Vipaśyin. He was preaching the Dharma for the assembly at that time.”
There was a son of a householder who came to the assembly and, hearing the Buddha speak of the merit of giving and observing the precepts, felt joy and faith.
He immediately received from the Buddha the three refuges and the precept against killing, and further offered a single coin as an offering to that Buddha.
For this reason, he has received blessings life after life; his wealth and treasures have been at his disposal, never lacking for anything.

The son of the elder at that time was none other than the present Bhikṣu Ghoṣila. Because of his gift of a single coin, he remained constantly wealthy in money and goods for ninety-one kalpas, continuing even into this present life.
Furthermore, because his parents from both families provided him with all necessities and he observed the precept against killing, he fell [into a favorable rebirth].
An aquatic creature swallowed by a fish did not die because it had received the Three Refuges; now, encountering me, it has attained the path of Arhatship.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (or *Saddharma-smṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*) states: Long ago, there was a man who was sold by another to be sacrificed to a deity by having his life taken.
Once he was bound and could not escape, he thought only of the Buddhas. Having uttered these words once—“Namo Buddhāya”—his life ended, and he was reborn in the [Heaven of] the Thirty-three.

For sixty kalpas, they shall enjoy supreme and wondrous bliss in the Heaven of the Thirty-three. The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha, saying, "By what cause and condition was this person born there?
The Buddha said, "At the time of death, he was endowed with pure goodness; he gave rise to a heart of pure faith and took refuge in the Tathāgata.
Because he uttered 'Namo Buddha' but once, this person immediately planted deep roots of merit. Furthermore, for eighty..."
Throughout the kalpas, one attains the knowledge of past lives; in every place of rebirth, one is free from all afflictions and brings all suffering to rest.
The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: "Even one who utters 'Namo Buddha' once, by virtue of this root of goodness, shall enter the realm of nirvāṇa in a manner that is inexhaustible."

The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "If there are sentient beings who cultivate goodness and, with a pure mind, take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, even for the duration of a finger-snap, without giving rise to any other thought, they will, at the end of life, be reborn in the White Maṇi Heaven. There, they will indulge their desires in the five sensory pleasures and experience joy in their hearts and minds.
By virtue of the merit of the Three Refuges, until their retribution is exhausted, they shall attain Nirvāṇa in future lives. — Upāsaka...

The *Saijie jing* (Sūtra on the Precept of Restraint) says: Whether one is a layperson or a monastic; whether it be the three refuges, the eight precepts of the fast, the five precepts, or the full set of precepts;
whether they are complete or incomplete; whether for a single day, a single night, a single moment, a single thought-instant, or for as long as one lives.
Receive and uphold this with a sincere heart. You should know that such a person attains great merit and virtue. The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* says:
"A person who upholds the precepts would rather sacrifice their own body and life than ever violate them. Why is this?

Because the precepts are the primary foundation of the Path, the sublime destination for the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava*), and the level road to the peace and bliss of Nirvāṇa. If one upholds the pure precepts, when calculating their merit, it is immeasurable and boundless."

It is boundless, like the great ocean. Just as the great ocean is the dwelling place of many great beings such as asuras, tortoises, aquatic creatures, and makaras, so too is the ocean of precepts the dwelling place of the great beings of the three vehicles.

Just as the great ocean abounds in gold, silver, and the seven treasures, so too does the ocean of precepts produce many wholesome dharmas, including the four applications of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.

The various dhyānas and samādhis—such treasures as these—are like the great ocean, with a foundation of vajra and surrounded by vajra mountains, into which the four great rivers flow without increasing or decreasing. The ocean of precepts is likewise: the vinaya serves as its foundation.
The Abhidharma Mountains surround it, and the rivers of the four Āgamas flow into it, remaining serene and constant, neither increasing nor decreasing.
For what reason does this ocean receive these inflows yet neither increase nor decrease? It is because the fires of the Avīci Hell flow downward into it.
It surges upward toward the great ocean; because the seawater evaporates and dries up, it does not increase. Because it constantly flows in, it does not decrease.
Likewise, the ocean of the Buddha’s Dharma and precepts does not increase because of heedfulness, nor does it decrease because of the possession of merit.

Therefore, one should know that those who are able to uphold the precepts possess exceedingly great virtue. As stated in the *Sūtra on the Measurement of Merit through Rare Occurrences*: At that time, the Elder...
The Elder Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "If a virtuous man or woman is able to speak thus:
'I now take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, I take refuge in the Saṅgha,' how much merit do they obtain? I truly do not understand; I pray that the Buddha will explain it."
"May all sentient beings attain right knowledge and vision. The Buddha told Ānanda, "I shall explain this for you.
Suppose the continent of Jambudvīpa were filled with *srotāpannas* (here translated as 'those who have entered the stream,' the first stage of the noble ones).
If there were a son or daughter of good family who, for a full hundred years, provided them with every kind of worldly object of entertainment and enjoyment that exists."
He gives gifts to them, further providing complete offerings through the four requisites—robes, food, bedding, and medicinal requisites—and pays them respect and prostrations.
Even after their parinirvāṇa, he collects their relics and erects stūpas made of the seven precious substances, making various offerings with incense, flowers, music, banners, and flags.
What do you think, Ānanda? Would the merit obtained be great or not? Ānanda replied to the Buddha, "It would be very great, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
The Buddha said: "It is not as if someone, with a pure and sincere mind, were to say: 'I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
The merit obtained thereby would surpass that previous merit such that the latter would not equal even one-hundredth part of it; nor one-thousandth, nor one-ten-thousandth part;
indeed, it cannot be reached by any calculation, analogy, or metaphor. The Buddha told Ānanda: "Suppose the western continent of Aparagoyānī were filled with these..."

As for the *sakṛdāgāmin* (here translated as "Once-returner," the noble one of the second fruit), suppose someone were to provide offerings to each one of them for a full two hundred years, just as described previously.

Furthermore, this does not equal the merit of the Three Refuges. Even if the Pūrvavideha continent were filled with Anāgāmins (here translated as "Non-returners," the third-stage noble ones), and someone were to provide offerings to each one for three hundred years as previously described, it still would not equal the merit of the Three Refuges.
Even if the Uttarakuru continent were filled with Arhats, and someone were to [provide offerings] for four hundred...
For a year, even if one were to make offerings to each of them individually as described before, it would still not equal the merit of taking the Three Refuges.

Even if the four continents were filled with Pratyekabuddhas, and someone were to make offerings to each of them individually for ten thousand years as described before, it would still not equal the merit of taking the Three Refuges. Even if the entire trichiliocosm were filled with Tathāgatas, Buddhas...
Suppose there were someone who, for twenty thousand years, made offerings as described above one by one, thereby acquiring immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable merit;
yet this would still not equal the merit obtained by another person who, with a pure and sincere heart, says these words:

"I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, I take refuge in the Sangha. The merit gained by the latter surpasses that of the former a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and ten-thousandfold. It is not so.
It can be calculated; it can be known through words, analogies, and categories.

Furthermore, Ānanda, if there is someone who is able to take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha—even for as long as a single snap of the fingers—and is able to receive the ten wholesome deeds and, having received them, practice them, by this cause and condition they shall obtain immeasurable and boundless merit. Moreover, if there is another person...
If one can, for a single day and night, receive the eight precepts and practice accordingly as taught, the merit obtained will surpass the previous merit by a thousandfold,
ten-thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-millionfold, and even to the extent that it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.

If one can receive and uphold the five precepts for as long as life lasts and practice according to the teachings, the merit obtained will surpass the previous blessings by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold—beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.
Furthermore, if there is someone who receives the śrāmaṇera precepts or the śrāmaṇerī precepts, it is even more superior than the former. Furthermore, if there is someone who receives...

The Śikṣamāṇā precepts are superior to the former. Furthermore, if there is someone who receives the full Bhikṣuṇī ordination and practices in accordance with the precepts, they are again superior to the former.

Moreover, if there is someone who maintains the full Bhikṣu precepts for as long as life lasts, practicing according to the teachings as prescribed—without deficiency, without transgression, and without defilement—practicing the pure Brahma-faring, they shall attain the immeasurable.
Its boundless merit exceeds the former by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, and even a hundred-thousandfold;
it is beyond reach of calculation or analogy. Upon hearing this teaching on the three refuges, Ānanda vowed to protect the great bhikṣu precepts for the rest of his life.
Seeing that the merit was immeasurable, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. The Buddha told Ānanda, "The name of this sutra is..."
"Rare, rare indeed is this sutra! You should receive and practice it accordingly. Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Ānanda rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Brahmin again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, please bestow upon me the Dharma of the Three Refuges. Then the Heavenly Lord dispatched three benevolent deities.

"The sixteen great kings have protected and assisted my body; having already received the compassionate salvation of the World-Honored One, I now prostrate once more and request to receive the precepts.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, brahmin! You should purify your body, speech, and mind, and with a sincere and earnest heart,"

The Method for Respectfully Receiving the Precepts: The Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time all attained their realization through the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
O Brahmin, for as long as life lasts, you shall not kill living beings, nor shall you instruct others to kill. Can you maintain this precept?
If you are able to uphold this, there are five divine kings who will follow and protect your person, ensuring that malevolent spirits and evil ghosts find no opportunity to harm you.
Brahmin, for as long as life lasts, do not steal the wealth or treasures of others, nor instruct others to commit theft.
Can you uphold this precept? If you can uphold it, there are five virtuous divine kings who will follow and protect your person, Brahmin.
"For as long as life lasts, do not engage in sexual misconduct. Can you uphold this precept?

If you can uphold it, five divine kings will follow and protect your body, and all demons shall find no opportunity against you. Brahmin, for as long as life lasts, do not speak falsely or engage in frivolous speech."
"Divisive speech and inciting strife—can you observe this precept? If you can observe it, five divine kings will follow and protect your person.
Brahmin, for as long as life lasts, do not drink grain liquor, sugarcane liquor, grape liquor, or any intoxicating spirits that lead to heedlessness."
Such liquors as these must not be drunk at all. Can you uphold this precept? If you can uphold it, five benevolent deities will follow and protect your person.
Brahmin, this is the Dharma of the Three Refuges and Five Precepts. You should uphold it well; do not violate it.
The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* says: "Good son, the precepts of an upāsaka are extremely difficult to maintain."
Why is this? Because these precepts can serve as the foundation for the śrāmaṇera precepts, the mahābhikṣu precepts, and the bodhisattva precepts, up to and including unsurpassed bodhi.
