The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "Some may ask: 'There are other immeasurably grave dharmas;

for what reason did the Buddhas of the past not prohibit those, yet prohibit alcohol? Good son, because of drinking alcohol, the sense of shame and remorse is destroyed, and one does not give rise to fear regarding the three evil realms.
For this reason, one is unable to receive the remaining four precepts. Therefore..."

The Buddhas of the past have established the prohibition against drinking. Some may ask: "Since the Tathāgata has already spoken of the many faults of alcohol, why was it not mentioned at the beginning of the five precepts?
This interpretation is incorrect. Why? Because such a precept regarding alcohol is called a "prohibitive heavy" (*pratikṣepa-guru*) rule, not a "natural heavy" (*prakṛti-guru*) rule.
The Tathāgata first established the natural heavy precepts, and subsequently established the prohibitive heavy ones. Furthermore, the Tathāgata...
One clearly understands the nature of all phenomena; therefore, this is established. The *Upāsaka-śīla-lakṣaṇa-sūtra* states:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "There are three ways of committing the offense of killing that take human life: first, doing it oneself; second, commanding another; and third, dispatching a messenger."
"Acting oneself" means taking one's own life or taking the life of another. "Instructing others" means saying to another person, "Seize this person, bind them, and take their life.
"Sending a messenger" means saying to another, "Do you know so-and-so? Seize this person, bind them, and take their life.
When the messenger takes that person's life according to these instructions, at that time the upāsaka commits an unforgivable offense (*ānantarya-karma*). Furthermore, there is...
There are three types: first, using internal matter; second, using non-internal matter; third, using both internal and non-internal matter. Regarding the first, using internal matter to kill:
this refers to using the hand to strike, or using the foot, or other parts of the body, to cause another to die. This constitutes an offense of irreparable transgression (*āpatti-pārājika*).
If the person does not die immediately, but later dies as a result of this [action], it likewise constitutes an offense of irreparable transgression. If, however, they do not...
Because of death, this offense is one that can be confessed. Second, regarding killing by means of external matter:

if a person causes another to die using wood, stones, knives, spears, bows, arrows, or the like, they incur the same offense as before. Third, regarding killing by means of both internal and external matter:

if one takes hold of wood, stones, or the like with the hand and strikes until death occurs, the offense incurred is the same as before. Furthermore, there are cases where it is not [by these means...]

These three types of killing consist merely of mixing various poisons and placing them in the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or on clothing, or within food, bedding, and so forth, causing the victim to die;

this constitutes the same offense as before. If a lay follower (*upāsaka*) intentionally constructs a fire pit and someone falls into it and dies, he commits an offense that cannot be rectified (*ānantarya*).
If a non-human being, such as a spirit or ghost, falls into it and dies, he commits an intermediate offense.

It is a transgression that may be confessed. If an animal dies, one commits a minor offense that may be confessed. If no one dies at all, one commits three preparatory offenses that may be confessed as light transgressions.
If one resolves in one's mind solely to create a fire pit for a person and does not extend it to others, yet a person falls into it and dies, one commits an offense that may not be confessed;
if they do not die, one commits a preparatory offense. If a non-human or an animal dies, there is no offense. If [it is] a *yū*... [text ends].

A lay follower may, through the karma of speech, cause death by means of incantations; or they may praise death and extol it; or they may, as a person of physical strength, give rise to an evil thought with the intent to cause death;
or they may cause an abortion to bring about death. Regarding the gravity of the offense incurred in these cases, it is all to be judged according to the same principles as previously stated.

As for those who do not commit an offense: if one accidentally causes the death of another by dropping wood, stones, or the like while walking, coming, going, or entering and exiting, it does not constitute an offense.
The rest is as explained in the Sūtra. Second, regarding the precept against stealing: taking the heavy property of another through three modes constitutes an offense that cannot be atoned for.
First, the application of the mind; second, the application of the body; third, the removal from its original place. Regarding the first, the application of the mind:

it refers to the arousal of thought and reflection with the intent to commit theft. Regarding the second, the application of the body: it refers to using one’s physical parts or limbs to take another’s property.

Regarding the third, the removal from its original place: wherever the object may be located, lifting it and placing it elsewhere constitutes a grave offense. Furthermore, there are three ways of taking:

Regarding objects of great value: one commits an offense of non-expiation (anantarya) through five ways of taking another's property of great value: first, taking it oneself; second, instructing another to take it; third, sending a messenger to take it;

furthermore, there are five other ways of taking another's property of great value that constitute an offense of non-expiation: first, taking it through harsh coercion; second, taking it with contempt; third, taking it by falsely assuming another’s name;
fourth, taking it by forceful seizure; fifth, taking what has been entrusted to one. As for "objects of great value," if one steals [an object worth] five...

Money. If one obtains property worth five *māṣakas*, one commits an offense that cannot be remedied (*anivārya-āpatti*). Furthermore, there are seven conditions for taking another's property that constitute such an offense:
first, the perception that it is not one’s own; second, the absence of consent; third, not taking it temporarily; fourth, knowing there is an owner; fifth, being not insane;
sixth, being not mentally deranged; seventh, being not impaired by illness. If these seven conditions are met and one takes another’s valuable object, one commits [the offense].
It is not an offense involving remorse (*anavaśeṣa*). To take another’s property worth less than five *māṣaka* coins that is light in value constitutes an offense involving remorse (*sāvaśeṣa*).

Conversely, regarding the seven types of taking another’s property mentioned above, one commits no offense whether the value is heavy or light. The third precept, the precept against sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*), has four aspects.
First, males; second, females; third, eunuchs (paṇḍaka); fourth, those with both sexual organs (ubhayavyañjana). As for females: human females, non-human females, and female animals.
As for males: human males, non-human males, and male animals. Eunuchs and those with both sexual organs each likewise have three types, as previously described.

If an upāsaka engages in sexual intercourse with a human female, a non-human female, or a female animal through the three orifices—namely, the mouth and the two lower orifices—he commits an offense that cannot be atoned for.
This applies equally to a human male, a non-human male, a male animal, a eunuch, or a hermaphrodite.

Engaging in sexual intercourse through two locations—the mouth and the anus—constitutes an offense that is irreparable (anāpatti). If one has formed the intention but has not yet engaged in sexual intercourse and the union has not occurred, one commits a minor offense that is repentable (duṣkṛta).
If the two bodies have come together but one stops before engaging in sexual intercourse, one commits an intermediate offense that is repentable (sthūlātyaya).
Apart from these three locations, engaging in sexual intercourse through any other location constitutes an offense that is repentable. This applies whether the partner is a human or an animal.

If one whose physical faculties are not yet impaired engages in sexual misconduct at those three locations, they commit an offense that cannot be remedied (*anivārya*); the minor offenses are as described above.

If a person, though not having received the precepts, violates a follower of the Buddha who maintains the pure precepts, although they do not incur the specific guilt of breaking the precepts, they shall never thereafter be able to receive the five precepts, the eight precepts, or even the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) for leaving the household life. This also applies if one is insane or mentally deranged.
"Enveloped by pain and affliction, one who does not realize this incurs no offense. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "I have two bodies: first, the birth-body; second, the precept-body.

If a son of good family were to erect for my birth-body a stupa made of the seven treasures reaching as high as the Brahma-heaven, yet someone were to damage it, that offense could still be repented. But to damage my precept-body, its offense is immeasurable. Thus he spoke.

The offense is like that of the nāga king Elāpattra; it is an unforgivable transgression. One who violates the pure precepts commits a sin equal to the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*); because the evil karma is so heavy, it obstructs the Noble Path.

Therefore, he is not permitted to go forth [into homelessness]. Regarding the fourth precept against false speech: The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "I have reproached false speech in various ways and praised those who do not speak falsely.
One should not speak falsely even in jest; how much less so when speaking falsely intentionally.
Within this, an offense occurs if a lay follower (*upāsaka*), without knowing or seeing it, claims for himself the superhuman states of noble dharma (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
He says, "I am an Arhat, one who has attained the fruits of the four [immeasurables], up to the four dhyānas;

I have attained loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, as well as the four formless absorptions, the contemplation on impurity, and mindfulness of ānāpāna. Gods and nāgas come to my presence and make offerings to me."
If one asks me about a matter and I answer that question, I commit an offense of non-confession (anantarya). If, however, one has actually seen but says they did not see;

has actually heard but says they did not hear; has actually doubted but says they did not doubt; or if there is something but they say it is not, or there is nothing but they say it is—such minor lies constitute an offense of confession (pāyattika).
If one forms the intention to speak falsely but has not yet uttered the words, one commits a minor offense (dukkaṭa).

It may be confessed. To speak without fully expressing one's intent constitutes an offense that may be confessed. If one claims for oneself that one has attained the Path of the Sages, one commits an offense that cannot be confessed.

However, there is no offense if spoken while in a state of madness, mental derangement, or without conscious awareness. The *Adbhuta-dharma-paryāya* states: The Buddha told Prince Jeta, "There are two kinds of false speech: the grave and the light.

For the sake of receiving offerings, one outwardly displays diligence while inwardly practicing what is crooked and turbid, speaking falsely to others. One might claim to have attained the realm of dhyāna, or say that one has seen the Buddha, seen a nāga, or seen a ghost. Such a person [commits a grave offense]."

This is called a great lie. One who commits this offense falls into the Avīci Hell. Furthermore, lying can cause people to be killed and families to be destroyed. There is also lying that violates agreements and pacts, causing others to harbor resentment; such is called a minor lie, for which one falls into the minor hells.

Other instances—such as joking, or matters involving concealment and secrecy where one says there is something when there is nothing, or says there is nothing when there is something—do not constitute a violation of the precepts. The fifth precept concerns intoxicants:

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "If you say, 'I am a disciple of the Buddha,' you must not drink alcohol—not even a single drop on the tip of a blade of grass may be drunk. There are two kinds of alcohol: grain-based alcohol and wood-based alcohol.
Grain-based alcohol is that which is made from various five grains mixed with rice. Wood-based alcohol is that which is made from roots, stalks, wood, leaves, or fruits."

Various seeds, medicinal herbs, and miscellaneous ingredients used to make liquor—whatever possesses the color, fragrance, and taste of alcohol, and which can intoxicate a person when drunk—is called "alcohol.
If one tastes it even by swallowing a single mouthful, it is also termed "drinking. If one drinks grain-based liquor (surā), one commits an offense with every swallow.
If one drinks fermented vinegar-based liquor (śukta), or sweet liquor (madhu), or eats yeast (kiṇva) that can intoxicate a person, or eats dregs (kaṣāya)... [and so forth].

Regarding the dregs of wine: if one drinks that which resembles wine—possessing the color, fragrance, and taste of wine, and capable of intoxicating a person—one commits an offense with every swallow.
However, if it merely has the color of wine but lacks its fragrance and taste, and is incapable of intoxicating a person, as well as other such drinks, there is no offense.
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, if a sick bhikṣu or similar person is not cured by other medicines, [he may take it].
There is no offense if the alcohol is used as medicine. There is no offense for one who is insane, mentally deranged, suffering from pain, or unconscious.

In the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, the Buddha said: "Because of killing, all sentient beings obtain in the present life an ugly appearance, weak strength, a bad reputation, a short lifespan, the depletion of wealth and property, separation from their kin, the reproach of the noble and holy ones, and lack of trust from others."
When another person commits a transgression, one suffers its calamity unjustly; this is called the fruit of evil karma in the present life.
After casting off this body, one shall fall into hell and undergo much suffering and affliction—such as hunger, thirst, a long lifespan, an ugly appearance, weak strength, and an ill reputation;
these are called the fruits of evil karma in future lives. Even if one obtains a human body, one will again suffer from an ugly appearance, a short life, and poverty.
It is exhausted. By the power of the causes and conditions of such an evil person, all external five-grains, fruits, and gourds will completely diminish.

The calamity of this person flows forth to affect the entire world. Good son, if a person delights in stealing, that person will likewise obtain an ugly appearance, weak strength, an evil reputation, and a short life;
their wealth and goods will dwindle, their kinsmen will be separated from them, and others will lose their property.
One harbors doubts within oneself; though one associates closely with others, they do not place trust in them; and one is constantly rebuked by the wise and the noble.
This is called the fruit of evil karma in the present life. After casting off this body, one falls into hell and receives an ugly appearance, meager strength, and an ill repute;
one suffers from hunger and thirst for a vast duration of life. This is called the fruit of evil karma in future lives.
If one obtains a human body, one will be destitute of wealth; though one may acquire it, it is lost immediately thereafter.

One will not be loved or cherished by parents, brothers, wives, or children, and will constantly experience physical suffering with a mind filled with grief and affliction. This is due to the power of the causal conditions of such an evil person.
Whatever all the people eat and consume, they shall derive neither beauty nor strength; this is the evil fruit of that person, and its calamity flows upon the myriad people, O son of good family.
Furthermore, if there is a person who delights in false speech, that person will in the present life obtain foul speech and an ugly appearance.
Although what they say is true, people do not believe or accept it; everyone hates them and takes no pleasure in seeing them.
This is called the retribution for evil karma in the present life. After casting off this body, they enter hell and undergo great suffering, tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat.
This is called the retribution for evil karma in future lives. Even if one obtains a human body, one’s mouth will be incomplete;
though what one says is true, people will not believe or accept it, and those who see one will find no pleasure in it. Although one speaks the True Dharma, people will take no delight in hearing it.
Because of the causal power of such an evil person, all external material assets and resources will diminish. Good son, if there is yet another person...

Those who delight in drinking alcohol will, in this present life, take pleasure in squandering their wealth; they will suffer many physical and mental ailments; they will constantly delight in strife and contention;
their ill repute will spread far and wide; they will lose their wisdom; their minds will be devoid of shame and remorse; they will possess an ugly complexion and weak strength;

they will be constantly rebuked by all; people will take no pleasure in seeing them; and they will be unable to cultivate goodness. These are called the evil retributions of drinking alcohol in the present life.
After casting off this body, one dwells in hell and undergoes immeasurable suffering such as hunger and thirst; this is called the fruit of evil karma in future lives.
If one obtains a human body, the mind is constantly deranged and unable to maintain mindfulness or contemplate wholesome dharmas.
Due to the causal power of this evil person, all external objects and assets will rot and decay.
Good son, if there is another person who delights in sexual misconduct, that person will be unable to protect their own body, the bodies of others, or any sentient beings.
Upon seeing this, everyone conceived doubts. Regarding the deeds they had committed, falsehood was their primary characteristic;

at all times, they constantly experienced suffering and affliction, their minds were perpetually distracted, and they were unable to cultivate virtue. They delighted in losing their wealth and property, and even their wives and children no longer felt any affection or longing for them.

A short lifespan is called the present evil fruit of sexual misconduct. After casting off this body, one dwells in hell, experiencing an ugly form and strength, suffering from hunger, thirst, and a long life of immeasurable affliction; this is called the retribution for evil karma in future lives.

If one obtains a human body, yet possesses an ugly appearance and foul speech such that people do not wish to see him, and is unable to protect his wife, concubines, sons, or daughters—due to the causal power of being such an evil person, he shall have no mastery over any external objects. Good son!
There are five places where one who has received the Upāsaka precepts should not frequent: the houses of butchers, prostitutes, taverns, kings, and Caṇḍālas.
Son of good family, there are five things that one who has received the Upāsaka precepts should not do:
first, not selling living beings; second, not selling swords or blades; third, not selling poisons; fourth, not...

Selling alcohol. Fifth, one must not press oil (in foreign lands, there are insects within the hemp; therefore, it is an offense. In this region, there are no such insects; thus, one should not be guilty of the offense).
Good son, having received the Upāsaka precepts, there are furthermore three things that one must not do: first, one must not make nets;

second, one must not use indigo for dyeing (in foreign lands, the five major colors are dyed [with indigo], which kills many insects. In this region, though blue is dyed differently, it also kills many insects and is counted among the five major colors); third, one must not...
One obtains fermented skins. Good son, having received the Upāsaka precepts, there are two further things one should not do:
first, gambling with dice, go-boards, or *ṣaḍyūta*; second, various forms of singing, dancing, and musical entertainment.

Good son, having received the Upāsaka precepts, there are four kinds of people whom one should not associate with: first, those addicted to board games and gambling; second, those who drink alcohol; third...
Deceiving others; fourth, selling intoxicants. Good son, for one who has received the Upāsaka precepts, there are conditions of negligence that must not be indulged in.
What constitutes negligence? It is when one is cold, hot, hungry, thirsty, or full from overeating;
at dawn or dusk; when distracted; while working; when first intending to work; when losing [an opportunity]; when afraid; when joyful; or during times of banditry, famine, or high grain prices.

At times of illness, at times of youth, at times of old age, at times of wealth, at times of poverty, and at times when one’s life or property is at stake—if you do not cultivate wholesome dharmas during such times, can you truly avoid [the consequences]?
Son of good family, having received the Upāsaka precepts, you must first study worldly affairs;
once you have mastered them, seek wealth in accordance with the Dharma. If you obtain wealth, divide it into four parts: one part should be used for offerings.
One's parents, oneself, and one's wife, children, and retinue—of these, two parts should be used for lawful trade and commerce;
the remaining one part should be set aside and accumulated for one’s own use as a basis for making merit. Good son, wealth should not be entrusted to four types of persons:
first, the elderly; second, those in distant places; third, wicked people; and fourth, those with great power. To these four types of persons, one should not entrust [one's wealth].
Appendix: Good son, there are four types of evil persons whom one who has received the Upāsaka precepts should always avoid: first, those who delight in speaking of the faults of others;
second, those who delight in speaking of false views; third, those whose mouths are soft but whose hearts are evil; and fourth, those who do little but speak much.
Such precepts are also called the "Initial Stage," the "Guiding Stage," the "Level Stage," and the "Equal Stage."
It is called the Ground; it is also called the Ground of Loving-kindness, the Ground of Compassion, the Footprint of the Buddha, the Root of All Meritorious Qualities, and the Field of Blessings.
For these reasons, the wise should uphold it and not disparage it. Furthermore, there are two fruits of the precepts:
first, the bliss of the devas; second, the bliss of Bodhi. The wise should seek the bliss of Bodhi, and not [the bliss of the devas].

[They] seek the pleasures of the various devas. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are three grades of upholding the precepts (*śīla*). If one upholds the precepts at the lower level, one is reborn among human beings.

If one upholds them at the middle level, one is reborn among the devas of the six desire realms (*ṣaḍ-kāmadhātu*). If one upholds them at the superior level, and further cultivates the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), one is reborn among the devas of the form and formless realms (*rūpa-dhātu* and *ārūpya-dhātu*).
Regarding the superior upholding of the precepts, there are three types: by upholding the precepts with lower purity, one attains the state of an Arhat.
Middle-purity observance of the precepts leads to the attainment of a pratyekabuddha; superior-purity observance of the precepts leads to the attainment of the Buddha-way.
Being unattached and non-reliant, unbroken and unimpaired, and praised and cherished by the noble ones—this is called superior-purity observance of the precepts.
If a person seeks great and wholesome benefit, they should firmly uphold the precepts as if cherishing precious treasures or protecting their own life. Why is this? For example, like a great...
The earth: all things in the universe depend upon the earth to abide. Precepts are likewise the dwelling place for all wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, it is impossible for one who has no feet to walk, no wings to fly, or no boat to cross over. If one lacks the precepts yet desires to seek excellent fruits, it is just like that.
If a person abandons these precepts, even if they dwell in the hardships of the mountains, [they will find no merit].
Their conduct—eating fruit and taking medicine—is no different from that of birds and beasts. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that those who do not receive the Buddha’s precepts are called "beasts.
In every place where they are born, they do not see the Triple Gem; like wood or stone, they lack a mind, and are thus called "non-Buddhists" (*tīrthika*).

Those who hold wrong views are no different from pieces of wood. Therefore, a sutra says: "To summarize all meritorious qualities and practices that aid the Path, they have precepts as their foundation and the observance of precepts as their beginning.
Because the precepts are pure, one does not sever the lineage of the Buddha and achieves equal and perfect enlightenment;
one does not sever the lineage of the Dharma and discerns the nature of phenomena; one does not sever the lineage of the Sangha and cultivates the unconditioned path."
Because they maintain pure precepts in an uninterrupted succession, the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states:
"If one can wholeheartedly receive and uphold such precepts, this person is called a *puṇḍarīka* lotus among upāsakas;
the most subtle and supreme fragrance among upāsakas; a pure lotus among upāsakas; and a true, precious jewel among upāsakas."
"O noble sons, among upāsakas there are great men. As the Buddha has taught, there are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
the first is the householder, and the second is the renunciant. A renunciant bodhisattva is called a bhikṣu; a householder bodhisattva is called an upāsaka.
For a renunciant bodhisattva to uphold the monastic precepts is not difficult; however, for a householder bodhisattva—"
To uphold the precepts of a householder is indeed difficult. Why is this? Because householders are entangled by many adverse conditions.

(Now, these five precepts must be received from a virtuous and enlightened teacher before one can truly obtain them. If the teacher is not enlightened, they will be unable to instruct one on what to refrain from and what to practice, or what constitutes an offense and what is a transgression—these being the essentials for transcending the world.

Therefore, their transmission is necessary; one must follow the teachings of the Dharma. As stated in the *Vibhaṅga-sūtra*: Ānanda asked the Buddha, "If at a time there is no enlightened teacher to transmit the teachings and the precepts, and if there is someone who has written out the Vinaya and bestows it upon another, may that person attain deliverance and enter the Path? The Buddha replied: "If one receives the precepts from such a person, one does indeed become a follower of the Way. )

"No," the Buddha said. "Only those who have fully understood the prohibitive Dharma may be conferred the precepts. It cannot be received through mere words; only then does it accord with the Dharma. Why is this? Because the Buddha is the one of supreme wisdom in the heavens above and the world below; he must not be transmitted recklessly so as to lose the essential meaning."

All must be clear regarding the precepts, laws, and prohibitions, thoroughly mastering every detail before conferring them upon others. To confer the precepts upon others while lacking clarity regarding the essential matters of the precepts and prohibitions violates the Buddha’s faith in the precepts; to do so while considering it correct is no small transgression.

The *Xi-gou jing* (The Sutra of the Mad Dog) says: The Buddha said to Ānanda, "In the future, during the final age, there will be disciples who act as teachers yet are indolent and lack wisdom. They do not refine themselves in the Buddha-dharma, yet they desire the offerings of others and perform the rite of bestowing precepts upon them;

this is called 'selling the precepts. They flatter and follow after others. When they see someone greedy for killing, they do not admonish them; when they see someone addicted to wine, they do not cause them to abstain from it, saying that one may drink a little. Teachers who instruct in such a manner cast people into the *naraka* hells. Ānanda asked the Buddha, "If those who have newly resolved their minds encounter [such teachers]..."

"A bad teacher, being ignorant and lacking understanding, claims that such is the nature of the Dharma, leading others to believe and accept his words. Out of folly and lack of comprehension, one follows him. If such a person later encounters a true master, may they receive the precepts again? The Buddha said: "Within my Dharma, which is vast and expansive, it is entirely possible to repent. One may further purify oneself through confession.

When first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, the mind was constantly shrouded in darkness; having been misled by a bad teacher, one truly did not know. To receive the precepts again is the very beginning of entering the Dharma.

At the time when one does not know and lacks understanding, one is not a disciple of the Buddha, but merely a person of minor virtue in the world who possesses no great merit. The Elder Sūnāra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva has already received the upāsaka..."
Regarding the precept on restraint: how, furthermore, should one make offerings to the Triple Gem? The Buddha said: "Good son, there are three kinds of fields of merit in the world:
first, the field of gratitude; second, the field of merit; and third, the field of the poor. The field of gratitude refers to parents, teachers, elders, and preceptors.
The field of merit refers to those who have attained the stage of 'warmth' (ūṣmagata), up to those who have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi. As for the field of the poor: it refers to all those who are destitute, suffering, and in distress.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, constitutes two kinds of fields: first, the field of gratitude; second, the field of merit.
The Dharma is likewise these two kinds of fields. The Saṃgha consists of three kinds: first, the field of gratitude; second, the field of merit; and third, the field of the poor. By means of...
For this reason, a bodhisattva who has already received the upāsaka precepts should, with a sincere and diligent mind, make offerings to the Triple Gem.

Good son, the Tathāgata is the treasury of all dharmas; therefore, the wise person should, with a sincere and diligent mind, make offerings to the living body, the parinirvāṇa body, the physical image, and the stūpas and temples. Even in wilderness places where no stūpas or temples exist, one should always...
Maintain mindfulness with reverence and offer praise. Whether performing the act oneself, encouraging others to do so, or seeing others perform it, one should give rise to joy in the heart.
If one possesses the power of merit, one should extensively teach many people to perform it together.
Once the offering has been made, one should not harbor thoughts of self-importance regarding one’s own person, nor should one [behave otherwise] toward the Triple Gem.
Thus it is. In all acts of offering, one does not employ others to perform them, nor does one do so for the sake of surpassing others. While performing them, one feels no regret;
the mind is free from anxiety or distress. One joins the palms in praise, showing reverence and respect.

Whether with a single coin or immeasurable jewels, whether with a single thread or immeasurable threads, whether with a single flower or immeasurable flowers, whether with a single incense or immeasurable...
Regarding the measure of incense: whether it be a single verse of praise up to immeasurable verses; whether it be a single prostration up to immeasurable prostrations;
whether it be circumambulating once up to immeasurable times; whether it be for a single moment up to immeasurable moments;
whether performed alone or together with others—O son of good family, if one can thus make offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha with a sincere heart, [the merit is immeasurable].
Whether I am present now or after my parinirvāṇa, there is no difference between them. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"If one makes an offering of even a single incense stick or lamp to the Buddha-dharma, or even presents a single flower, one shall dwell in the Immovable Land (*Acalā*). One who properly guards the property of the Buddha and the Saṃgha [shall likewise attain this]."

If one sweeps and cleans the grounds of the Buddha and the Sangha, or makes images and stupas even as large as a thumb, and constantly gives rise to a joyful heart, one will likewise be born in the Land of Immovability (the Land of Immovability is the Eastern realm of Akṣobhya Buddha). This is the Pure Land, eternally adorned and unmoved by the three calamities. The Buddha told Sujāta:
"If one makes offerings to the Sangha, this is equivalent to making offerings to both the Buddha and the Sangha treasures. If one contemplates the merits of the Buddha-Dharma..."
This is subtle and profound; it is the complete fulfillment of making offerings to the Triple Gem. If, when giving, one does not seek karmic retribution, this is the offering of unsurpassed bodhi.
It fully matures the *dānapāramitā* (perfection of giving), cultivates the path to awakening, and enables one to attain immeasurable merit in the future.
It can likewise bring about both self-benefit and the benefit of others. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "At that time, the Buddha..."
The maternal aunt Mahāprajāpatī offered a supreme golden robe to the Buddha. The Buddha exhorted her to give it to the Saṃgha, for they alone can properly digest and receive such offerings.
Thus we know that regarding the Jewels of the Buddha and the Saṃgha, there is no difference in the merit produced. The Buddha spoke this verse:

"If a person reveres and loves the Buddha, they should likewise revere and love the Saṃgha; one should not make distinctions, for both are equally jewels. — *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* (The Treatise on Great Adornment).
It is said: "The ocean of merit of the Sangha is such that none can measure it. Even the Buddha gave rise to joy and reverence, praising it himself with a hundred verses;
how much more so should all other people not offer praise? This vast and excellent field of merit yields great benefit from even a small sowing.
Therefore, one should make offerings to the Sangha—with equal mind toward both the elderly and the young—and should not harbor discrimination."
[The Buddha] replied, "It is so. The Buddha told Sujāta: "Good son, if a person delights in giving, that person destroys five harmful and evil dharmas:
first, wrong view; second, lack of faith; third, negligence; fourth, stinginess and greed; and fifth, anger and delusion."
Having abandoned these evils, joy arises in the mind. Because of this joy, one eventually attains true and perfect liberation.
This person obtains four rewards in the present life: first, everyone—even enemies—finds them pleasing to behold;
second, their good reputation spreads throughout the four quarters; third, when entering a great assembly, their heart is free from fear; fourth, [they attain...]
All virtuous people delight in coming to associate with him. Good son, when one practices giving for oneself, his mind feels no regret.
Even if such a person should fall into hell due to adventitious afflictions, although he dwells in that evil place, he experiences neither hunger nor thirst.
By these causes and conditions, he is freed from two kinds of suffering: first, the suffering of iron balls; second, the suffering of molten iron. If he takes on the body of an animal...
They will easily obtain [necessities] and lack nothing. If they have the body of a hungry ghost, they will not suffer from hunger or thirst but will always remain satiated.
If they obtain a human body, their lifespan, physical form, strength, peace and happiness, eloquence, as well as their faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom, shall surpass all others.
Even though they dwell in an evil age, they will not commit evil deeds; when unwholesome dharmas arise, they will never follow after or accept them. In...
In places of fear, one does not give rise to terror. If one receives a celestial body, ten matters are preeminent;
furthermore, one should deeply contemplate the suffering of poverty and the happiness of the noble and wealthy. For this reason, fix the mind and always delight in practicing giving.

Good son, if a person possesses wealth but, upon seeing a seeker, says they have nothing or that they are destitute, you should know that this person has already declared their own poverty in future lives.
Of meager virtue. Such a person is called negligent. Good son, it is not the case that a person without wealth says, "I have no wealth. Why is this?
For there is no human being who does not possess water and grass; even though one may be a sovereign of a nation, [these are still present].
It is not that one must necessarily be able to give. Although one may be poor, it is not that one cannot give. Why is this? Even a poor person has their share of food;
after eating, if they wash their vessel and give away the rinsed water to those who ought to eat it, they likewise obtain merit and virtue.
If one gives even a speck of flour to an ant, one also obtains immeasurable fruit and retribution of merit. Who in the world is so utterly poor as to [lack such things]?
"Is there not even this much dust of parched flour? Who is there whose life would not be preserved by eating three morsels of parched flour in a single day?
Therefore, all people should give half of their food to beggars. Good son, as for those who are utterly poor, who is there so naked that they have no clothes?
If they do have clothes, how could they not give even a single thread to tie a wound on someone's finger?"
"Permit me to give wealth. Shall I provide the wick for the lamp? "Good son, among the people of the world, who is so poor as to be without a body?
If one possesses a body, upon seeing another performing meritorious deeds, one should go to assist them with joy and without weariness;
such a person is also called a donor and shall likewise obtain merit. At times they may receive a portion, at times an equal share, and at times even a superior share. For this reason..."
For this reason, when I accept food from King Prasenajit, I offer prayers for both the king and the poor, so that the merit they obtain is equal and without distinction.
Good son, it is like a person who buys incense—ointment incense, powdered incense, scattered incense, and burning incense.

Regarding these four types of incense, whether someone touches them, buys them, or measures them, they all smell the same without distinction; yet these various fragrances do not lose even a hair’s breadth of their quality.
The merit of practicing generosity is also like this: whether it be much or little, coarse or fine, [the result remains the same].

If one assists with the body out of a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), or if one sees or hears from afar and gives rise to a heart of joy—because the mind is equal in these cases, the resulting retribution (*vipāka*) will have no difference.

Son of good family, if one possesses no wealth and, upon seeing another give, does not feel joy or faith but instead harbors doubts regarding the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), this is called poverty. If one has abundant wealth and treasures, possessing them freely and without hindrance...
A fertile field of merit that lacks internal faith and cannot offer gifts is also called "poor. Therefore, the wise person, according to whatever they have, gives as much as their strength permits.
Apart from giving, there is nothing else that can lead one to the happiness of gods and humans, up to the unsurpassed bliss.
For this reason, I have said in the sūtras: "The wise person observes for themselves; even if only a single morsel of food remains," and so forth.
If one eats it, one lives; if one gives it to another, one dies. One should still give it away, how much more so if there is an abundance?

Son of good family, a wise person should contemplate that wealth is impermanent. Because it is impermanent, throughout immeasurable lifetimes it has been lost, destroyed, and diminished, yielding no benefit.
Yet, although it is impermanent, it can bring about immeasurable benefit. Why then be stingy and not distribute it?

"Is it through giving? Furthermore, the wise person observes the world: if there are those who maintain the precepts and possess great learning, by the power of the causes and conditions of maintaining the precepts and great learning, they may even attain the fruit of Arhatship.
Yet, although they have attained this fruit, they cannot eliminate sufferings such as hunger and thirst.
If an Arhat finds it difficult to obtain lodging, clothing, food and drink, bedding, or medicine for illness, it is all due to..."

Due to the causes and conditions of not practicing giving in previous lives, those who have broken the precepts—if they delight in practicing giving—will, even though they fall into the realms of hungry ghosts or animals, always obtain full satisfaction and lack nothing. Good son, apart from the practice of giving, one cannot attain two fruits:
first, sovereignty; second, liberation. Even if those who uphold the precepts are born in the heavens, if they do not cultivate giving, [they will not attain these fruits].
Therefore, one must not consume superior food or exquisite necklaces. If a person desires worldly happiness as well as unsurpassed bliss, they should delight in giving.

The wise should contemplate that birth and death are boundless, and the experience of pleasure is likewise so; for this reason, one should practice giving to sever birth and death, rather than seeking the enjoyment of pleasure.
Furthermore, one should reflect: although one may possess the wealth of the four continents, [it is still impermanent].
Even when dwelling on the [heavenly] grounds and experiencing immeasurable bliss, one still knows no satisfaction.
Therefore, I ought to practice giving for the sake of supreme bliss—not for the sake of humans or devas. Why? Because they are impermanent and finite. (Supreme bliss is the bliss of supreme nirvana.
Good son, once the gift has been given, one should simultaneously transform sentient beings. How does one transform them? Upon seeing those who are impoverished, one should first speak to them...
He says: "Are you able to take refuge in the Three Jewels? Will you receive the precepts of the fast (upavāsa)?

If they say they can, first cause them to receive the three refuges and the precepts of the fast, and afterwards bestow the gift. If they say they cannot, one should further say to them: 'If you cannot...'"
"Are you able to follow my words and say that all phenomena are impermanent, without self, and that nirvāṇa is tranquil extinction?
If you say you can, I shall first instruct you and then bestow the gift. If one can thus instruct first and give later, they are called a great donor.
If one gives clothing, one obtains exquisite color; if one gives food, one obtains unsurpassed strength; if one gives lamps, one obtains purity.
Sudarśana, if one gives with a vehicle, one receives peace and happiness in this body; if one gives with a dwelling, one lacks for nothing that is required.
Good son, when a wise person gives, it is not for the sake of karmic retribution. Why is this? Because they know with certainty that this cause will necessarily yield its fruit.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "If a person observes the precept against killing for one day and one night, they will certainly not encounter the outbreak of the calamity of weapons in future lives.
Furthermore, if one offers a single *harītakī* fruit to a sick monk with a profound and pure mind,"
In future lives, one will certainly not encounter the outbreak of the calamity of pestilence.
If one gives even a single morsel of food with a profound and pure mind to the Saṃgha, in future lives one will certainly not encounter the outbreak of the calamity of famine.
For this reason, the Venerable Bakula, having once received the precept against taking life, obtained the fivefold reward of immortality; he gave [medicine] to a sick bhikṣu.
By giving a single *harītakī* fruit, he enjoyed happiness and prosperity among gods and humans for ninety-one *kalpas*, never suffering from illness.
Now, in his final birth, he left the household life and became an Arhat; at the age of one hundred and sixty, he remained free from disease. This was due to his gift of one fruit to the Saṃgha.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that within a single thought-moment one can practice the six *pāramitās*; this refers to the time of practicing generosity (*dāna*).

Giving away wealth in accordance with the Dharma is the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*). Bestowing gifts while dwelling securely in the great path of goodness, without turning toward the two vehicles (*yāna*), is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). When afflictions such as stinginess or demons and the like arrive, being unable to disturb the mind is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Giving without ceasing is the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). Gathering the mind so that it does not scatter and remaining free from doubt is the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*). The perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) is the realization that all phenomena are empty and signless. This is called the six perfections. Furthermore, when one practices these six perfections, one should not seek the fruits of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; rather, one should dedicate them solely to supreme, perfect enlightenment. This is called the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya-pāramitā*). Not abandoning the thought of awakening even amidst the various sufferings of saṃsāra is the perfection of resolve (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*). Even if one attains the stage of non-retrogression, never forgetting the original vow is the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*). Being able to manifest all manner of bodies according to the inclinations of sentient beings is the perfection of knowledge (*jñāna-pāramitā*). These are called the ten perfections. Furthermore, regarding the four foundations of mindfulness: contemplating the body as impure is the perfection of ethical discipline; contemplating feelings as suffering is the perfection of patience; contemplating the mind as impermanent is the perfection of diligence; and contemplating phenomena as selfless is the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, regarding the four right efforts: exerting effort to abandon unwholesome states already arisen is the perfection of generosity; exerting effort to prevent unwholesome states not yet arisen is the perfection of ethical discipline; exerting effort to cultivate wholesome states not yet arisen is the perfection of patience; and exerting effort to increase wholesome states already arisen is the perfection of diligence. Furthermore, regarding the four bases of psychic power: possessing the basis of concentration through the desire-to-act is the perfection of generosity; possessing the basis of concentration through the energy-to-act is the perfection of ethical discipline; possessing the basis of concentration through the mind-to-act is the perfection of patience; and possessing the basis of concentration through the investigation-to-act is the perfection of diligence. Furthermore, regarding the five faculties: the faculty of faith is the perfection of generosity; the faculty of energy is the perfection of ethical discipline; the faculty of mindfulness is the perfection of patience; the faculty of concentration is the perfection of diligence; and the faculty of wisdom is the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, regarding the five powers: the power of faith is the perfection of generosity; the power of energy is the perfection of ethical discipline; the power of mindfulness is the perfection of patience; the power of concentration is the perfection of diligence; and the power of wisdom is the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, regarding the seven factors of enlightenment: the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness is the perfection of generosity; the factor of enlightenment of energy is the perfection of ethical discipline; the factor of enlightenment of joy is the perfection of patience; the factor of enlightenment of tranquility is the perfection of diligence; the factor of enlightenment of concentration is the perfection of wisdom; the factor of enlightenment of equanimity is the perfection of skillful means; and the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena is the perfection of knowledge. Furthermore, regarding the eightfold noble path: right view is the perfection of generosity; right intention is the perfection of ethical discipline; right speech is the perfection of patience; right action is the perfection of diligence; right livelihood is the perfection of wisdom; right effort is the perfection of skillful means; right mindfulness is the perfection of resolve; and right concentration is the perfection of power. Furthermore, regarding the three gates of liberation: the gate of emptiness is the perfection of generosity; the gate of signlessness is the perfection of ethical discipline; the gate of wishlessness is the perfection of patience; the gate of non-arising is the perfection of diligence; the gate of non-existence is the perfection of wisdom; the gate of non-self is the perfection of skillful means; the gate of non-duality is the perfection of resolve; and the gate of non-manifestation is the perfection of power. Furthermore, regarding the three trainings: training in higher ethical discipline is the perfection of generosity; training in higher mind is the perfection of ethical discipline; and training in higher wisdom is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three liberations: the liberation of emptiness is the perfection of generosity; the liberation of signlessness is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the liberation of wishlessness is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three knowledges: the knowledge of the past is the perfection of generosity; the knowledge of the future is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the knowledge of the present is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma: the first turning is the perfection of generosity; the second turning is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the third turning is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three refuges: taking refuge in the Buddha is the perfection of generosity; taking refuge in the Dharma is the perfection of ethical discipline; and taking refuge in the Sangha is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three jewels: the Buddha-jewel is the perfection of generosity; the Dharma-jewel is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the Sangha-jewel is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three kinds of giving: the giving of material things is the perfection of generosity; the giving of the Dharma is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the giving of fearlessness is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of precepts: the precept of restraint is the perfection of generosity; the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the precept of benefiting sentient beings is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of patience: the patience of enduring injury is the perfection of generosity; the patience of accepting suffering is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the patience of contemplating dharmas is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of diligence: the diligence of practice is the perfection of generosity; the diligence of cultivation is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the diligence of teaching is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of concentration: the concentration of emptiness is the perfection of generosity; the concentration of signlessness is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the concentration of wishlessness is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of wisdom: the wisdom of hearing is the perfection of generosity; the wisdom of reflection is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the wisdom of cultivation is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of merit: the merit of giving is the perfection of generosity; the merit of morality is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the merit of meditation is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of roots of goodness: the root of goodness of giving is the perfection of generosity; the root of goodness of morality is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the root of goodness of meditation is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of liberation: the liberation of the śrāvaka is the perfection of generosity; the liberation of the pratyekabuddha is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the liberation of the bodhisattva is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of vows: the vow to benefit oneself is the perfection of generosity; the vow to benefit others is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the vow to benefit both oneself and others is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of aspirations: the aspiration for wealth is the perfection of generosity; the aspiration for the Dharma is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the aspiration for liberation is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of intentions: the intention of compassion is the perfection of generosity; the intention of loving-kindness is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the intention of equanimity is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of thoughts: the thought of renunciation is the perfection of generosity; the thought of non-hatred is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the thought of non-delusion is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of conduct: the conduct of body is the perfection of generosity; the conduct of speech is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the conduct of mind is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of purity: purity of body is the perfection of generosity; purity of speech is the perfection of ethical discipline; and purity of mind is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of adornment: the adornment of body is the perfection of generosity; the adornment of speech is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the adornment of mind is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of protection: protecting oneself is the perfection of generosity; protecting others is the perfection of ethical discipline; and protecting both is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of accumulation: the accumulation of merit is the perfection of generosity; the accumulation of wisdom is the perfection of ethical discipline; and the accumulation of both is the perfection of patience. Furthermore, regarding the three types of reliance: relying on
To be without regret is the *dhyāna-pāramitā*. That both giver and receiver, as well as the material object itself, are ultimately ungraspable is the *prajñā-pāramitā* (*dāna* means giving).
Furthermore, it is said that there are three kinds of giving: first, the gift of material wealth; second, the gift of the Dharma; and third, the gift of fearlessness.
To restrain oneself through the observance of precepts so as not to encroach upon the property of any sentient being is to practice the gift of material wealth. It is able to...
To preach various teachings so as to bring about awakening is called the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*). Sentient beings fear death;

to maintain the precepts and refrain from harming them is called the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*). The *Mahāpuruṣa-śāstra* states: "The gift of wealth removes the physical suffering of sentient beings; the gift of Dharma..."

The giving of material wealth removes the suffering of the minds of sentient beings; the giving of the Dharma brings about physical happiness. The giving of material wealth brings about mental happiness.
The giver of material wealth is beloved by sentient beings; the giver of the Dharma is revered by the world. The *Adbhuta-dharma Sūtra* states:

Giving food provides relief for one day’s life; giving wealth and goods provides relief for the deficiencies of an entire lifetime. Preaching the Dharma and teaching others can cause sentient beings to enter the supramundane path.

The *Fayuan* states: "If one causes others to transcribe [the scriptures] using paper and ink, or if one transcribes the Tathāgata’s authentic canon oneself and subsequently gives it to others so that they may read and recite it, this is called the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*). Thus it is said.
The giver, in future lives, will attain a superior physical form, enjoy an extended lifespan, possess abundant wealth and treasures, and experience great strength and peace of body.
They will obtain unimpeded eloquence and clear confidence in the faith. Therefore, know that the gift of Dharma is superior and surpasses the gift of material wealth.
If one hears that the gift of Dharma surpasses the gift of material wealth, the foolish person does not understand this; they instead conceal their wealth and take pleasure only in it.
Regarding the recitation of sutras: if it is as described above, it is not equal to someone who, with an understanding mind, gives a single coin in charity;

this surpasses one who, with a deluded mind, recites hundreds of thousands of millions of scrolls of sutras. Therefore, when the Tathāgata established his teachings, his intention lay in both understanding and practice;

only through their dual cultivation does one attain the fruit of Buddhahood. The *Abhidharma-amṛta-rasa-sūtra* says: "If one gives to an animal, one receives retribution for a hundred lifetimes. If one gives..."
If one gives to an unwholesome person, one receives retribution for a thousand lifetimes. If one gives to a wholesome person, one receives retribution for ten million lifetimes.

If one gives to an ordinary person who has transcended desire, one receives retribution for a hundred billion lifetimes. If one gives to a person who has attained the Path, one receives retribution for incalculable lifetimes.
If one gives to a Buddha, one attains Nirvana. The *Saṃghāṭa Sūtra* states: The great assembly addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the merit of a single Buddha..."

"What is the measure of this merit? The Buddha said, "It is like the atoms of the great earth; it is like all sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each becoming a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage.
Even the sum of all the merits possessed by all such Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage does not equal the power of the merit of a single Buddha.
The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* says: "If an upāsaka can constantly go to the monastery..."

One who associates with the bhikṣus and others, inquires about the flavor of the Dharma, listens and receives it with a sincere mind, remembers it without forgetting, is able to discern its meaning, and transforms sentient beings—such a person is called an upāsaka.
He benefits both himself and others. If one is unable to practice and study in this way, [he is not].
One who speaks as described above— disrespecting bhikṣus, seeking out their faults while going to listen to the Dharma,
lacking faith and reverence, serving non-Buddhists, perceiving their merits, and placing deep faith in the sun, moon, the five planets, and the various lunar mansions— is an upāsaka [only in name].

It is not called being firm; it is dwelling in accordance with the Dharma. If a person, for the sake of protecting their home, body, and life, performs sacrifices and offerings to various deities, that person is not said to have lost their refuge in the Dharma.
This is provided that the person, with a sincere heart, believes that [the Triple Gem] can save them from all fears.
If one pays homage to non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas), that person immediately loses the refuge in the Triple Gem.

However, if one hears that among the various devas there are those who have previously seen the Buddha and whose merit surpasses one's own, and thus pays them homage and makes offerings, this person does not lose the method of refuge.
At times, when paying homage to heavenly kings, one should do so as one would pay homage to worldly kings, elders, nobles, the aged, or persons of virtue.
Even though you may pay homage to them, you must be careful never to accept the teachings of their false views. When making offerings to the gods, you should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
For the sake of protecting your life, wealth, kingdom, and people from fear, why would you not reject the false views they preach?
A wise person should observe what the non-Buddhists say: that all things in the world are created by Īśvara.
"It is the work of Heaven. If it were indeed the work of Heaven, for what reason would I now cultivate these wholesome karmas?
All sentient beings perform good and evil deeds, and by the conditions of those karmas, they themselves receive their retributions.
Furthermore, you claim that all things—seasons and constellations—are created by Maheśvara. How can I accept such false teachings? O Wise One!
Clearly understanding this, one knows it to be the fruit of karma. Why, then, would one say that time, the stars, or Maheśvara create it?
For these reasons, the wise do not accept the false and erroneous teachings of the non-Buddhists. Good son, all sentient beings...
In accordance with one's karmic actions: those who cultivate right view experience peace and happiness, while those who cultivate wrong view undergo great suffering and affliction.

By virtue of cultivating wholesome karma, one attains great sovereignty; having attained sovereignty, sentient beings draw near to one, and one further proclaims for them the causes and conditions of wholesome karma.
It is through the causes and conditions of wholesome karma that one attains sovereignty; all sentient beings likewise attain it by means of cultivating the wholesome.
It is by reason of karmic causes and conditions that one attains peace and happiness, not because of the influence of the year or the stars. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"The various celestial deities do not dare to seek offerings or prostrations from lay followers (*upāsaka*), just as a sovereign of a nation certainly does not seek them from bhikṣus, for they fear it would impair their merit and lifespan.
As a sūtra says, regarding the Northern Heavenly King (*Virūpākṣa*): [text continues].
He invited the five hundred noble monks, including Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Śāriputra, to his own palace. Having prepared offerings for them, he requested that they grant him verses of aspiration.
He further entreated them, saying: "From this day forward, may all those who have gone forth as well as lay followers and others [be protected]."
When they arrive at my temple, all should offer me verses of aspiration.

We, along with our retinues, shall from this time forth protect and uphold the True Dharma with single-minded devotion, ensuring that the Buddha’s monastic and lay disciples are forever free from harm at all times.
Then the Venerable One, having granted their request as requested, addressed all those—both monastics and laypeople—who had received the Buddha’s precepts:

When entering a celestial temple, one should always offer praises and aspirations to the deity in accordance with the Dharma; however, there has never been a precedent for requiring one to join the palms in reverent salutation.

If a lay follower were to delight in prostrating to celestial deities, they would be no different from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), as they would be engaging in the activities of those who cherish and follow false teachers.
By means of such practices, they draw near to false masters, thereby strengthening the causes for falling into the evil realms.
It flourishes. From this point on, it spreads from one to another until many lifetimes have passed, and they likewise take pleasure in such wrong conduct.
Furthermore, if a lay follower (*upāsaka*) pays homage to celestial deities, he leads many sentient beings to great ruin. Those who worship the deities all say:
"This lay follower is deeply learned in the Buddha's teachings; now that he comes to pay homage to the deities we serve, he must surely harbor respect for these heavenly gods."

Excellent! We have taken refuge without error. Furthermore, those in the world who seek the correct principles of happiness investigate the Buddha’s teaching, yet fail to exhaustively realize its truth.
Observing this, they give rise to perverse attachments, claiming that the Buddha’s teaching resembles worldly secular texts;
because it cannot refute [their own] false doctrines, they cause such people to return once more to taking refuge in the various celestial deities. Thus it is said:

[By doing so,] one causes immeasurable sentient beings to increase their false attachments; this is called a great decline and loss. Furthermore, lay followers (upāsaka) do not bind themselves to celestial deities;
rather, they are merely leading a band of heretics to submit [to them]. Lay followers should pay respect to those who are not renunciants. Therefore, [the rule applies specifically to] lay followers.

One should not pay homage to any celestial deities. (Regarding the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, which permits lay followers [upāsakas] to prostrate before celestial deities as they would before a sovereign or similar figures, one must not believe or accept its assertions.

Following the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, even such homage is prohibited; if even the Heavenly Kings do not permit it to be paid, how much less so for other ghosts and spirits? Nowadays, there are those who believe in and accept forged texts such as the *Yuhuang Baogao*, the *Sanguan Jing*, the *Qidou Jing*, and the *Shousheng Jing*.

Is this not a great error? Someone might say: "Although these scriptures are not authentic, they can be used to induce people toward goodness; what fault could there be in this? The answer is: Have you not heard that "if the ground is not true, the fruit will be crooked"? To fail to attain right view in life after life is a fault that is by no means small. You ought to act with haste.

By means of their power, they go there to take birth, or they travel by means of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to listen to the Dharma.

During the Tang Dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Cimin traveled in person to India to seek out Sanskrit manuscripts and visit virtuous teachers. Deeply weary of Jambudvīpa, he then reflected to himself:
He asked: "In which country or region is there joy without suffering? By what dharma and what practice can one quickly behold the Buddha?

He questioned all the Tripitaka masters of India, and they all praised the Pure Land, which accorded with the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha]. Having heard this, he received it upon the crown of his head with reverence.
Gradually proceeding to the northern regions of India, to the kingdom of Gandhāra, there was a great mountain to the northeast of the royal city. On that mountain was a statue of Avalokiteśvara.

you must exhort others to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, recite the sutras, and dedicate their vows [toward rebirth there]."
He was reborn there. Having arrived in that land, he beheld the Buddha and me; he would naturally have known that the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land surpasses all other practices.
Having spoken thus, he suddenly vanished. Furthermore, during the second year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, the Dharma Master Fazhao resided at Yunfeng Temple in Hengzhou.
Endowed with compassion, forbearance, precepts, and meditative concentration, he was revered by his contemporaries. One day, two times in succession, [visions] appeared within his alms bowl.

Later, when he went to Mount Wutai, he beheld extraordinary light. Indeed, he found Zhulin Monastery; it was approximately twenty li in circumference and contained one hundred and twenty courtyards.
All were adorned with jeweled stupas, and the ground was made entirely of pure gold. Flowing channels and flowering trees filled its interior, radiating light.

He entered the monastery and went to the lecture hall, where he saw Mañjuśrī in the west and Samantabhadra in the east, each occupying a lion throne and preaching the Dharma while surrounded by a multitude of ten thousand people.
Daoyao prostrated himself and asked: "In this final age, ordinary beings are far removed from the Sage;

those who serve as spiritual friends have become increasingly inferior, and our defilements and obscurations are even deeper. The Buddha-dharma is vast and profound; I do not know which dharma gate one should cultivate most effectively."
It is the most swift and essential method. Mañjuśrī declared: "Among all gates of practice, none is equal to the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti).

"Even up to all the Buddhas, they are all born from mindfulness of the Buddha. Therefore, know that mindfulness of the Buddha is the king of all dharmas.
You should practice mindfulness of the Unsurpassed Dharma King without ceasing. Zhao then asked, "How should one practice this mindfulness? Mañjuśrī replied:
"To the west of this world is Amitābha Buddha. The power of that Buddha’s vows is inconceivable.
If you fix your mindfulness upon him, ensuring that your recollection is uninterrupted, you will certainly attain rebirth there and never fall back.

Having spoken these words, the two great sages each extended their golden hands and stroked the crown of Zhao’s head, bestowing upon him a prophecy of enlightenment. Overjoyed, Zhao prostrated himself in gratitude and withdrew. (Recitation of the Buddha’s Name)

Regarding the method for receiving the eight precepts of the fast (*upavāsa*), the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, "Today is the day of the fast.
Summon the upāsakas to bathe thoroughly, put on clean robes, and receive the *poṣadha*. The *Ekottarika-āgama* states: The Buddha addressed the upāsakas, "One should, during the eight..."
On the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the month, one should go to a senior bhikṣu and receive each of the eight precepts one by one;
receiving them one by one, do not allow them to be taken out of order. The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states:

"If an upāsaka, having already received and maintained the five precepts, is unable to receive and maintain the eight precepts on six days within a single month to make offerings to the Triple Gem, he incurs a fault."
This is a mental transgression. Therefore, the *Chān-fǎ* (Repentance Method) states: "To have no six fast days in a month is the work of indolence. The *Guǎngdìng jīng* (Guanding Sūtra) states:
